# qFT8

> Portable Amateur Radio, SWL, and SDR. qFT8 is a free FT8 app for Android, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux, with no ads and no account. Plug and play with more than 70 radios, the QMX and IC-7300 among them. FT8, FT4, FT2, LQ8, JS8, WSPR, CW, RTTY, SSTV and SSB, full AUTO, a live world map, POTA, SOTA and online logbooks, in 63 languages.

Current version: 3.24 (2026-11-08). Website: https://qft8.com/ (63 languages). Author: Luis Quesada Torres, HB9IPH.

## qFT8 at a glance

- Free, no ads, no account
- Android phones and tablets, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux
- Plug and play with 70+ radios
- Listening (SWL): SDR receivers, a heard log with SWL ADIF, SOTA and RAZA exports
- FT8, FT4, FT2, LQ8, Q65, MSK144, FST4, FST4W, JS8, WSPR, CW, RTTY, JTTY, SSTV, DRAW and SSB
- Full AUTO or one-click manual calling
- Its own decoders and encoders, written from scratch
- Live world map with real-time spots, POTA, SOTA, LQ8 activity and band propagation
- Award programmes and contests: POTA, SOTA, WWFF, IOTA, HEMA, GMA and more; ARRL Field Day and other contests (experimental)
- Integrates with QRZ, Logbook of the World, Wavelog, Cloudlog, qFT8log, HRDLog, HamQTH, HAMLOG.online, WRL, Club Log and eQSL; ADIF, SOTA and POTA
- Remote control from any browser
- 63 languages

## qFT8 in numbers

- 63 languages (64 language versions: English also has a British spelling); the website and the app are translated.
- 251 radio models from 33 brands (251 picker entries; one entry can cover several models, for example FT-991 / FT-991A): recognised over USB with CAT and audio set up by themselves, or keyed by VOX. Any other radio works through a VOX audio cable or a DigiRig.
- 130 modes in 67 mode-selector rows (family rows such as PSK, Olivia and the MFSK family stand for their sub-modes), in two tabs: HAM and SWL.
- 12 network radio protocols and 2 Bluetooth serial links; 17 SDR receiver types (listening only).
- 6 platforms: Android, iPhone and iPad (iOS), Windows, macOS, Linux and a web remote in any browser.

## Why people use qFT8

qFT8 is chosen for what it takes away: the computer, the interface box, the cables, the sign-ups and the cost. The reasons below are things the app does, each one checkable in the program or the user manual.

- **A whole station in a phone.** Plug the radio into an Android phone or tablet with one USB cable; qFT8 recognises it (251 models from 33 brands) and sets up CAT and audio by itself. No computer, no sound card, no interface box. The same program runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
- **Portable and field ready.** It keeps running with the screen off, is light on the battery, sets the clock from the internet or GPS and the locator from the phone's location, and decodes and transmits fully offline. Typical uses are POTA and SOTA activations, camping, travel and a small shack.
- **Free, no ads, no account.** No subscription, no login, no tracking; the program and every mode are free.
- **Easy for beginners, powerful for experts.** Full AUTO answers CQs, runs the QSO and logs it, with retry limits you control; or you call stations yourself with one tap. A first-start tutorial explains the screens. Experts get CAT consoles, transmit time limits, multi-tone, network radios and every setting.
- **Many modes in one app.** Weak-signal modes, Morse, teletype, keyboard modes, pictures, voice and a growing set of listening-only receivers, without switching programs.
- **Listen without a licence.** No callsign is needed: press SWL ONLY at the first start and use an SDR or any radio as a receiver, with a heard log, SWL reports and awards.
- **Logs go where you keep them.** Each QSO is sent to QRZ, Logbook of the World, eQSL, Club Log and other services as you log it, and to your logging programs on the network.
- **Your own language.** The app and website are in 63 languages.
- **LQ8 built in.** qFT8 sends and receives LQ8, a weak-signal mode with a four-message QSO, and shows who is on the air on a live map.
- **Control it from anywhere.** A browser, another phone or a second computer can operate the radio through the built-in web remote or the qFT8 bridge.

These themes come from the program's own store description and website. The Google Play review text could not be read from this build environment (the Play tools we use have no reviews access), so nothing here quotes or depends on reviews.

## What qFT8 is

qFT8 is "Portable Amateur Radio, SWL, and SDR": an all-in-one program for amateur radio operators and shortwave listeners, written and maintained by Luis Quesada Torres, HB9IPH. Decoders and encoders are its own, written from scratch; the decoder core is native code for speed on phones. It is for operating (calling, answering, logging, awards, contests) and for listening (SDR and radio receivers, a heard log, SWL reports).

- Platforms: Android 6.0 and newer (phones and tablets, Google Play and a direct download); Windows (64-bit and 32-bit, also from the Microsoft Store); macOS (every Mac, Apple Silicon and Intel); Linux (Intel/AMD and ARM, including the Raspberry Pi); iPhone and iPad (iOS, from the App Store; on an iPhone or an iPad without Apple silicon the radio transmits through its VOX); and a web remote that runs in any browser.
- Price and licence: free to use on any number of devices for personal, club and educational use; the licence file keeps the copyright (all rights reserved) and lists the third-party components. The user is responsible for holding a licence to transmit and for every transmission.
- Privacy: no ads, no tracking, no analytics libraries, nothing sold. Anything that sends personal data (callsign, locator, contacts) is opt-in. On its own the app only checks for a newer version and downloads public data (propagation, POTA and SOTA activity, LQ8 calls on the air, satellite orbits), without personal data. The web remote and the bridge are off until you turn them on. Full text: the privacy policy.
- Safety rules built in: only you can turn transmit on (the TX ON button), AUTO only works while you have it on, qFT8 never changes the radio's transmit power (you set that on the radio) and never transmits outside the amateur bands; transmit time limits protect the radio.

## How the mode selector is organised

The mode selector has two tabs at the top, HAM and SWL, and a PROBE button at their right. The tabs stay in place while the list scrolls, and the selector opens on the tab you used last. There is no third tab.

- **HAM tab: operating.** The amateur modes you can transmit: weak signal, beacons, keyboard and chat, classic radio, images, digital voice and packet (every mode is listed below). It also receives. The most used ones (FT8, LQ8, FT4, FT2, WSPR, JS8, RTTY, SSB, CW, SSTV) have a slightly lighter button so they are easy to find; experimental modes say so on a second line.
- **SWL tab: listening only.** Nothing here transmits. It holds the receivers: broadcast FM and AM, time signals, beacons and HF data, marine VHF, airband, AIS ships and ADS-B aircraft, weather satellites, radiosondes and weather alerts, pagers, balloons, weather stations, aero navigation aids, LoRa and Meshtastic, eLoran and more. Amateur signals you hear are listening too: the HAM tab's modes decode in receive-only form when the Ham features are off.
- **PROBE** is the AUTO MODE DETECTOR: it listens, names what is on the air and offers to switch to it. It is free to use whatever is switched on.
- **Greyed rows.** A mode your radio or SDR cannot do (the band is out of range, or the signal needs I/Q) is greyed, never hidden, and a tap says what is needed. When qFT8 cannot tell what a device can do, the row is offered.
- **Ham and SWL feature switches** (Settings, Features). With SWL off, only the HAM tab is shown. With the Ham features off, qFT8 is listening only: the HAM modes stay as receive-only, there is no transmit control anywhere, and the TX button turns red and reads NO CALLSIGN (a tap explains that transmitting needs a licence and a callsign, and SET UP asks for your callsign). First start without a callsign: press SWL ONLY.
- **A receiver holds the radio.** Opening a receiver that retunes a CAT radio (marine VHF, airband, a beacon or time-station receiver) turns TX off and the TX button reads NO TX / RX. Closing it puts the radio back on its frequency, and TX stays off until you press TX ON.
- **Which devices give I/Q.** SDRs (RTL-SDR on USB or on a network server, HackRF, Airspy, KiwiSDR, OpenHPSDR radios such as the Hermes-Lite 2, and others) give I/Q, so every receiver that needs it works within the SDR's frequency range and sample rate. Ordinary transceivers (IC-7300, IC-705, FT-891, K3, QMX and the like) give audio only: HAM modes, SSB, CW, AM and the audio receivers (time signals, NAVTEX, weather fax, HF data) work, while receivers that need I/Q (FM broadcast, AIS, ADS-B, sondes, weather satellites, sensors) are greyed with "needs an SDR". VOX and DigiRig are audio paths.
- **Awards.** qFT8 Awards, experimental, count only your own logs. HAM: ten stars each for modes, bands, DXCC entities and grid squares, with a table of modes by bands (472 stars in all) from every QSO you logged, confirmed or not. SWL: stations heard by amateur mode group and by service, DXCC and grids (140 stars). The diploma is generated from your log, nothing to apply for.
- **SWL logging.** Heard stations and receiver identifications (ships, aircraft, sondes, time stations, beacons) go into a separate SWL log, never mixed with your QSOs. The log page has a QSO / SWL dropdown, a filter bar and a first field QSO / SWL when you add an entry. Anything received through an SDR is logged as SWL by itself.

## Every mode (the mode selector, tab by tab)

Names marked (experimental) are experimental in the app; the others are stable. Counts: 130 modes in 67 rows.

### HAM tab: operating (transmit and receive)

**Weak signal (QSO)**

- FT8: The most used weak-signal mode: 15-second slots, one QSO in a few minutes, with full AUTO answering of CQ calls.
- LQ8: A weak-signal mode by HB9IPH described on lq8.org: a four-message QSO (CQ, call with locator and report, report with 73, 73), sent and received with full AUTO.
- FT4: The faster sibling of FT8 for contests and busy bands, with the same QSO screen and AUTO.
- FT2: An even faster mode of the same family, for short openings and strong signals.
- JT65 (experimental): The weak-signal mode used on HF and for moonbounce, with sub-modes A, B and C and one-minute periods.
- JT9 (experimental): A narrow weak-signal mode for HF and MF with one-minute periods.
- JT4 (experimental): A weak-signal mode for microwave and moonbounce work with sub-modes A to G.
- Q65 (experimental): A weak-signal mode for VHF, UHF and moonbounce with several sub-modes and period lengths.
- FST4 (experimental): A weak-signal mode with long periods for the low bands (LF, MF and the lower HF bands).
- MSK144 (experimental): A very fast weak-signal mode for meteor-scatter contacts on VHF.
- LQ4 (experimental): The faster sibling of LQ8: 7.5-second slots, the same four-message QSO, down to about -17.5 dB. Experimental.
- LQ2 (experimental): LQ4's frame at twice the speed: 3.75-second slots, the same four-message QSO, down to about -14 dB. Experimental.
- LQ16 (experimental): LQ8's frame at half the speed: 30-second slots, the same four-message QSO, the most sensitive of the family at about -24 dB. Experimental.

**Beacons**

- WSPR: Low-power beacon mode: qFT8 listens for beacons and transmits its own, and reports the spots to WSPRnet.
- FST4W (experimental): The beacon sibling of FST4: long periods for LF, MF and HF propagation checks.

**Keyboard / chat**

- JS8: Keyboard chat on a weak-signal waterfall: free text, directed messages and heartbeats.
- RTTY: Radio teletype (two alternating tones): send and read text; every RTTY signal in the passband is decoded at its own speed and shift.
- JTTY (experimental): A newer weak-signal text mode that runs on the RTTY screen.
- PSK (experimental) [PSK31, PSK63, PSK125, PSK250, QPSK31, QPSK63]: Phase-shift-keying keyboard modes: narrow, steady, conversational chat, from PSK31 up to PSK250 and the QPSK variants.
- FSQ (experimental) [FSQ 6, FSQ 4.5, FSQ 3, FSQ 2]: A keyboard mode for conversational and directed messages, with four speeds.
- IFKP (experimental) [IFKP 1.0, IFKP 0.5, IFKP 2.0]: A keyboard mode that sends text by incremental frequency keying, with three speeds.
- Olivia (experimental) [OLIVIA 8/250, OLIVIA 8/500, OLIVIA 16/500, OLIVIA 32/1000, OLIVIA 4/250]: A very robust keyboard mode (many tones, error correction) that reads below the noise, with five tone and bandwidth settings.
- Contestia (experimental) [CONTESTIA 4/250, CONTESTIA 8/250, CONTESTIA 16/500, CONTESTIA 32/1000]: A keyboard mode derived from Olivia with four tone and bandwidth settings.
- MT63 (experimental) [MT63 2000L, MT63 1000L, MT63 500L, MT63 1000S]: A keyboard mode that sends text on 64 tones at once, very resistant to fading and interference, with four settings.
- MFSK family (experimental) [MFSK16, MFSK32, MFSK64, MFSK8, MFSK11, MFSK22, MFSK128, THOR 16, THOR 11, THOR 22, THOR 8, DOMINOEX 11, DOMINOEX 16, DOMINOEX 8, THROB 1, THROB 2, THROB 4, THROBX 1, THROBX 2, THROBX 4]: The multi-tone keyboard modes MFSK (MFSK8 to MFSK128), THOR, DominoEX and Throb, picked beside the mode.
- Hell (experimental) [FELD HELL, SLOW HELL, HELL X5, HELL X9, FSK HELL, FSK HELL 105, HELL 80]: Feld Hell and its variants: each letter is sent as a small picture, readable by eye on the screen.

**Classic radio**

- SSB: Voice on single sideband, with voice memories.
- SSB I/Q (experimental): Single-sideband voice demodulated from the I/Q samples of an SDR (listening).
- CW: Morse: on-screen paddles, a keyboard, memories and a decoder for what you hear and what you key.
- AM: Amplitude-modulated voice on the amateur bands.
- AM I/Q (experimental): Amplitude-modulated voice demodulated from the I/Q samples of an SDR.
- FM: Frequency-modulated voice on the amateur bands.
- FM I/Q (experimental): Frequency-modulated voice demodulated from the I/Q samples of an SDR.

**Images**

- SSTV: Slow-scan television: send and receive pictures.
- DRAW: A picture drawn on the waterfall and sent as tones.

**Digital voice**

- FreeDV (experimental): FreeDV digital voice on HF (RADE V1, RADE V2, 700D, 700E, 1600, 700C; talk and listen), with qFT8's own modems, speech codecs and RADE engine.
- M17 voice (experimental): M17 digital voice, with qFT8's own Codec 2.

**Digital voice (data only)**

- DMR data (experimental) [DMR]: Receives the data of DMR (IDs, talkgroups, text, positions); voice is never decoded.
- D-STAR data (experimental) [D-STAR]: Receives the data of D-STAR (callsigns, text, positions); voice is never decoded.
- Fusion data (experimental) [Fusion YSF]: Receives the data of Fusion (YSF) (callsigns, text, positions); voice is never decoded.
- M17 data (experimental) [M17]: Receives the data of M17 (callsigns, text, positions).

**Packet / data**

- Packet (APRS) (experimental) [APRS 1200, HF PACKET 300]: APRS at 1200 baud on FM and HF packet at 300 baud, with an optional automatic acknowledge.

### SWL tab: listening only (nothing transmits)

**Broadcast**

- AM broadcast I/Q (experimental): Broadcast AM (long, medium and short wave) from an SDR's I/Q samples.
- FM + RDS I/Q (experimental): Broadcast FM from an SDR with the RDS station name and text.
- DAB / DAB+ I/Q (experimental): Digital radio (DAB and DAB+) from an SDR.
- DRM / DRM+ I/Q (experimental): Digital Radio Mondiale broadcasts from an SDR.

**HF utility**

- Time stations (experimental) [DCF77 / MSF / WWVB (time signals), WWV / CHU / JJY (time signals)]: Time-signal stations (DCF77, MSF, WWVB, WWV, CHU, JJY): decoded time and date.
- eLoran / DGPS (experimental) [Loran-C / eLoran, DGPS]: The 100 kHz navigation signals and the DGPS beacons of the long-wave band.
- Weather fax (experimental): Weather charts sent by radio facsimile, shown as pictures.
- NAVTEX / DSC / SITOR (experimental) [NAVTEX, DSC, SITOR-B, VHF DSC, SITOR-A]: Maritime text and calling: NAVTEX bulletins, digital selective calling and SITOR.
- Beacons / sounders (experimental) [NCDXF / IARU (Beacons / sounders), Chirp / CODAR (Beacons / sounders)]: Propagation beacons (the NCDXF / IARU network) and chirp sounders.
- HF data monitor (experimental) [ALE 2G, ARDOP, PACTOR-I]: Names and decodes headers of the HF data systems on the air (ALE, ARDOP, PACTOR-I).
- Selcall / tones (experimental) [CTCSS / DCS / DTMF (Selcall / tones), SELCAL (Selcall / tones)]: Selective-calling and sub-audible tones (CTCSS, DCS, DTMF) and SELCAL.

**Air and sea (public)**

- Airband voice (experimental): Aircraft voice between 118 and 137 MHz, 8.33 and 25 kHz channels.
- Marine VHF (experimental): Marine VHF voice and channels.
- ADS-B / UAT (experimental) [ADS-B (aircraft), UAT 978 (aircraft)]: Aircraft positions and identities, live on the map.
- AIS (experimental) [AIS (ships)]: Ship positions and identities, live on the map.
- VDES (experimental) [VDES ASM (ships)]: The VHF data exchange system for ships (ASM messages).
- Navaids (experimental) [VOR (Navaids), ILS (Navaids), DME (Navaids)]: Aero navigation aids: VOR, ILS and DME.

**Weather, sondes, satellites**

- Weather sats (experimental) [APT (weather satellites), Meteor LRPT (weather satellites), Meteor LRPT 80k (weather satellites)]: Weather-satellite pictures (APT and Meteor LRPT).
- Sondes (experimental) [RS41 (radiosondes)]: Radiosonde telemetry (RS41, DFM, M10 and M20, iMet, LMS6) with the flight on the map.
- Balloons (experimental) [Horus / SSDV (Balloons)]: High-altitude balloon telemetry and pictures (Horus).
- Weather stations (experimental) [Weather sensors]: Home weather sensors on the ISM bands (433, 868 and 915 MHz).
- Weather alerts (experimental) [SAME / EAS (weather alerts)]: NOAA SAME / EAS weather alerts.
- Amateur sats (experimental) [Satellite telemetry, BPSK 1200/2400 (Satellite telemetry), QO-100 (beacon lock, LNB drift)]: Amateur satellites (QO-100 and CubeSat telemetry) with satellite tracks.

**IoT and mesh**

- Pagers (experimental) [POCSAG (DAPNET) (amateur pagers)]: POCSAG pagers, including the amateur DAPNET channel.
- LoRa (experimental) [LoRa (Mesh networks)]: LoRa and Meshtastic packets.


PROBE, the AUTO MODE DETECTOR (a button at the right of the tabs): names what is on the air and offers to go to it.

Extras that apply to the modes: multi-tone (two signals in one transmission, experimental), a band selector that lists each mode's frequencies per band, and transmit time limits for every mode.

## LQ8

LQ8 is a weak-signal mode by Luis Quesada Torres, HB9IPH and described on lq8.org. A QSO takes four messages: CQ, call with locator and report, report with 73, 73; there is no R-report step and no RR73. qFT8 sends and receives LQ8, shows LQ8 activity on the map, can announce your own LQ8 calls, and lq8.org/live shows who is on the air. The encoder is locked to fixed test vectors, so every other qFT8 decodes our frames exactly as before.

251 radio models from 33 brands. qFT8 recognises these over USB and sets up CAT and audio by itself (or you pick the model in Settings). (experimental) marks the models that were added from the makers' documents and are not yet confirmed on air.

**Any other radio** works through a VOX audio cable or a DigiRig interface (audio only; qFT8 never changes the radio's transmit power).

**Network radios (no cable, no sound card):** Icom LAN / Wi-Fi, Kenwood LAN, Elecraft K4 Ethernet, FlexRadio SmartSDR, TCI (WebSocket), Rig server (rigctl protocol), FLrig (XML-RPC), SDR++ (rigctl + network audio), CAT over TCP (adapter), Serial server (RFC 2217), X6100 companion server, QuantumSDR (UDP).

**Bluetooth radios:** Bluetooth serial (SPP), Bluetooth LE serial.

**SDR receivers (listening only):** RTL-SDR (network), KiwiSDR (network), Hermes-Lite 2 / OpenHPSDR (network) (experimental), Airspy / RTL-SDR server (network, port 5555), remote SDR host (network: SDRplay, LimeSDR, Pluto ...), OpenHPSDR protocol 2 (network: ANAN, Saturn, Orion ...) (experimental), TCI IQ stream (network) (experimental), multicast RTP receiver (network, port 5006) (experimental), web receiver, audio channel (network) (experimental), wideband web receiver (network) (experimental), SDR++ server (network) (experimental), RTL-SDR (USB), Airspy HF+ (USB) (experimental), Airspy R2 / Mini (USB) (experimental), HackRF (USB, receive only) (experimental), ADALM-Pluto (USB network, receive only) (experimental), sound-card I/Q (SoftRock, FUNcube ...) (experimental).


## More about radios, CAT and SDR

- Every radio model is listed above, by brand; any other radio works through a VOX audio cable or a DigiRig interface.
- SDR receivers need no driver on the phone: an RTL-SDR dongle on the phone's USB (the V3 and V4 included, bias tee switch) works as plugged in; the full list of SDR types is above.
- The qFT8 bridge uses a radio connected to another of your devices, encrypted; the web remote lets a browser hear the radio and talk in SSB behind a private link and a password.

## Logging, services and events

- QSO syncing as you log: QRZ, Logbook of the World, eQSL, Club Log, HRDLog, HamQTH, World Radio League, HAMLOG.online, Wavelog, Cloudlog and qFT8log (one log shared between your own qFT8s). ADIF import and export. qFT8 never deletes a QSO on an online service.
- Logging programs on your network: the FT8 network log and ADIF over UDP, tested end to end with the common logging programs (named on qft8.com in the features list).
- Awards and activations: POTA and SOTA from the start (activate or hunt, count QSOs, spot yourself on POTA, export logs); experimental WWFF, WWBOTA, IOTA, SiOTA, HEMA, LLOTA, WWTOTA, RAZA, GMA and HOTA.
- qFT8 Awards: built in, for hams and listeners. Stars for modes, bands, DXCC entities and grid squares, a diploma generated from your own log (nothing to apply for) and achievements you can share.
- Contests (experimental): ARRL Field Day, Winter Field Day, ARRL RTTY Roundup, ARRL International Digital Contest, FT Challenge and EU VHF, with the exchange, duplicate checks, the score and a Cabrillo export. AUTO is off where the rules forbid automated QSOs.
- Map and spots: a live world map of every station you hear with distance and bearing, PSK Reporter and WSPRnet spots (your decodes are reported too), propagation, POTA and SOTA activations, satellite tracks and a compass.

## Listening (SWL)

No callsign is needed. With an SDR or an ordinary radio qFT8 decodes every mode it knows, logs what it hears into a separate SWL log (QSOs and signals like ships, aircraft and time stations, with the receiver used), exports ADIF, CSV, SOTA SWL and RAZA SWL files, reports to eQSL (SWL account), PSK Reporter and WSPRnet, and has its own SWL tutorial. SWL and ham logs are never mixed. SWL awards give stars for the stations you hear (140 stars); HAM awards have 472.

## Languages

The app and this website are available in 63 languages (the app also has a British English spelling): the languages are listed below. The TX button's words (TX ON, TX OFF, TUNE) stay in English everywhere.

## Questions and answers

### What is qFT8?

qFT8 is a free amateur radio program for weak-signal digital modes, Morse, teletype, pictures and voice. It runs on Android phones and tablets, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux, and can be controlled from any browser. It has no ads and needs no account. It is written by Luis Quesada Torres, HB9IPH, with its own decoders and encoders written from scratch.

### Why is qFT8 a good FT8 app for Android?

qFT8 is a complete FT8 station for Android 6.0 and newer, on phones and tablets: connect the radio with one USB cable and qFT8 recognises it and sets up CAT and audio by itself, with no computer and no interface box. It sends and receives FT8, FT4, FT2, LQ8, JS8, WSPR and more, answers CQs in full AUTO, keeps the clock right from the internet or GPS, shows every station on a live world map and logs each QSO to the services you choose. It keeps running with the screen off. Free, no ads, no account.

### Can I run qFT8 on a Windows, Mac or Linux computer?

Yes. qFT8 runs on Windows (64-bit and 32-bit, also from the Microsoft Store), on every Mac (Apple Silicon and Intel) and on Linux (Intel/AMD and ARM, including the Raspberry Pi), with the same modes, radios and features as on Android. The downloads on this page are free.

### Is there a qFT8 version for iPhone and iPad?

qFT8 also runs on iPhone and iPad (iOS). An iPhone or iPad cannot control a radio over a cable, so it keys the radio through the radio's VOX or through an audio interface that keys the radio from the audio.

### Which radios work with qFT8?

More than 70 radio models are plug and play over USB, among them the QRP Labs QMX, QMX+ and QDX, the Icom IC-7300, IC-705 and IC-9700, and radios from Yaesu, Kenwood, Elecraft, Xiegu, Lab599, GuoHe, FlexRadio and (tr)uSDX. Any other radio works through a VOX audio cable or a DigiRig, and SDR receivers such as an RTL-SDR can be used for receiving.

### Can I use a QRP Labs QMX or an Icom IC-7300 with my phone?

Yes. Plug the QMX, QMX+ or IC-7300 into an Android phone or tablet with one USB cable: qFT8 finds the radio, reads and sets its frequency over CAT, and sends and receives the audio over the same cable. No sound card or extra interface is needed. The same works with a computer.

### Which modes does qFT8 support?

FT8, FT4, FT2, LQ8, JS8, WSPR, CW, RTTY, SSTV and SSB, plus Q65, MSK144, FST4, FST4W, JT65, JT9, JT4, JTTY, PSK31, PSK63 and Olivia as experimental modes. LQ8 is a weak-signal mode created by HB9IPH that completes a QSO, with locator and signal report, in four messages.

### Does qFT8 work with POTA, SOTA, contests and online logbooks?

Yes. It shows POTA and SOTA references and live spots on the map and in the station list, counts your activation QSOs and exports ADIF; WWFF, IOTA, HEMA, GMA and other programmes, and contests such as ARRL Field Day, are experimental. Each QSO can go to QRZ, Logbook of the World, eQSL, Club Log, HRDLog, HamQTH, HAMLOG.online, Wavelog or Cloudlog as you log it, and to the logging programs on your network.

### Can I use qFT8 only to listen (SWL)?

Yes. qFT8 receives and decodes every mode it knows through an SDR receiver (an RTL-SDR dongle on an Android phone or a Linux computer, an RTL-SDR network server, your own or a public KiwiSDR, and other network SDRs) or through an ordinary radio in SWL mode, in which it never transmits. The QSOs you hear between other stations go to a heard log that exports SWL ADIF, CSV, SOTA SWL and RAZA SWL files. The user manual's SWL section explains the receivers and their drivers.
